Part B · Chapter B3

Loss and gradient descent

The loss measures a network's mistakes in one number, and gradient descent lowers it, usually a few examples at a time.

Training lowers the loss, one number that measures a network's mistakes. This chapter compares squared error with cross-entropy, which pushes harder when a sigmoid output is confidently wrong. It follows gradient descent, first for one sigmoid neuron on 268 spadenose sharks, then for hidden-unit networks, and shows how mini-batches and epochs change the path. The sharks are made up: records generated from published length-weight relationships, not field data.

You will need: gradient descent and the learning rate of A2, the log loss of A3, the gradient and chain rule, cross-entropy, and B1.

What the network is asked to minimise

Guess first. A network predicts a shark's weight, whether it is an adult, and which of five species it is. Should one loss serve for all three? Think about what a good loss does when the network is badly wrong.

The loss \(\ell\) of one example grows with the size of its mistake, and training adjusts the weights to lower the average loss. For a predicted number \(\hat y\) with label \(y\), the recorded value, a common loss is squared error \((\hat y - y)^2\). For two classes the network computes a score \(z\), and the sigmoid \(\sigma(z) = 1/(1+e^{-z})\) turns it into the probability \(p\) of "adult". A common loss for \(p\) is the cross-entropy, \(-\ln\) of the probability given to the true answer (\(\ln\) is the natural logarithm). The push is the slope of the loss with respect to the output score (\(z\) or \(\hat y\)). For squared error on a number, and for cross-entropy on a probability, the push is the prediction minus the label, times 2 for squared error.

  1. Compare the dots on the right plot, the pushes for a juvenile at \(z = +5\). Navy is cross-entropy, and coral is squared error on the same probability \(p\), with a smaller push.
  2. Drag \(z\) to −5: the navy push falls steadily, but the coral push first rises to about 0.30 near \(z = 0.7\).
  3. Choose "A number (weight, kg)" and drag the prediction: the push \(2(\hat y - y)\) is a straight line.
Task

For Tag 4127, a juvenile, at a score of +5 the push is 0.993 under cross-entropy and 0.013 under squared error, about 75 times smaller.

How it works

Take Tag 4127, a juvenile (\(y = 0\)), at \(z = +5\). The sigmoid gives \(p = 1/(1+e^{-5}) = 0.99331\) and \(1 - p = 0.00669\), so the network is confidently wrong, with 0.993 for "adult". Cross-entropy has a loss of \(-\ln(1-p) = 5.007\) and a push of \(p - y = 0.993\). Squared error has a loss of \((p - y)^2 = 0.987\) and a push of \(2(p - y)\,p(1-p) = 1.987 \times 0.00665 = 0.013\).

\(p - y\)cross-entropy push: 0.993|\(2(p - y)\)slope of the squared error on \(p\): 1.987×\(p(1-p)\)slope of the sigmoid on \(z\): 0.00665=0.013squared-error push

Common belief. Squared error is a good loss for any task, because it asks only for the output to be close to the label.

Why it fails. On a sigmoid output, the squared-error push contains the slope of the sigmoid, \(p(1-p)\), which is almost 0 where the sigmoid is flat, as at \(z = +5\). The cross-entropy push has no such factor, because the slope of \(-\ln(1-p)\), which is \(1/(1-p)\), cancels the factor \(1-p\) of the sigmoid's slope. Backpropagation computes the slopes of the loss on a network's weights by multiplying the push by other factors, so a tiny push usually gives small slopes.

Better account. Match the loss to the output: squared error for a number, cross-entropy for a probability. For several classes, softmax turns the scores into probabilities that add up to 1, and Go deeper works out the pushes \(p_k - y_k\) for five species.

Quick quiz

A network gives probability 0.25 to the true species out of five. What is the cross-entropy, and what is the cross-entropy of a model that guesses with equal probabilities?

\(-\ln 0.25 = 1.386\). A uniform guess gives 0.2 to the true species, so \(-\ln 0.2 = \ln 5 = 1.609\). The network is a little better than a guess.

For Tag 4127 at \(z = +5\), which push is larger, cross-entropy's or squared error's, and why?

Cross-entropy's, 0.993 against 0.013. The squared-error push contains the slope of the flat sigmoid, \(p(1-p) = 0.00665\), and the slope of the cross-entropy cancels that factor.

Go deeper number task, five classes, symbols, Python, debug tip about 8 min

The number task

Start with the first task. Tag 3305 weighs 0.228 kg, and a network that predicts 0.300 kg is 0.072 kg too high. The squared error is \(0.072^2 = 0.0052\) and the push is \(2 \times 0.072 = 0.144\). The loss is a parabola and the push a straight line, so a bigger mistake always gets a bigger push and there is no flat tail.

Targets of different sizes

A caveat for numbers is the size of the targets. A hammerhead of 53.889 kg predicted 10% too high is off by 5.389 kg, a squared error of 29.04. The same 10% miss on Tag 3305 is 0.0228 kg, a squared error of 0.0005. The big shark counts about 56,000 times more, so in a fit the largest animals would dominate the loss. Scaling the target to a spread of 1, as this chapter does, keeps the numbers small but multiplies all the errors by the same factor, so the ratio stays. A common remedy is to predict the log of the weight (A2). In logs a 10% miss costs \((\ln 1.1)^2 = 0.0091\) for a shark of any size.

Two classes

The second task is the one from A3, now seen from the point of view of a network. Choose "juvenile" and move the score to +5. The loss curves are the left panel, and the pushes the right one. Cross-entropy keeps pushing with a size close to 1 as the network gets more wrong. Squared error pushes with a size that rises to a peak of 0.30 near a score of 0.7 and then falls back to nearly 0, because the sigmoid is flat out there. Try "adult" with a score of −5 and the picture is mirrored.

Five classes

The third task has five scores and softmax (0.7). The made-up scores 2.4, 1.2, 0.5, −0.4 and −1.8 give probabilities 0.655, 0.197, 0.098, 0.040 and 0.010. If the true species is the hammerhead, the loss is \(-\ln 0.040 = 3.22\), and the pushes \(p_k - y_k\) are 0.655, 0.197, 0.098, \(-0.960\) and 0.010. The true species has a negative push, so its score is raised. The others have positive pushes, so their scores fall. The five pushes add up to 0, because the five probabilities add up to 1 and so do the five labels.

A loss is an average

A loss is also an average over many examples. Take the four sharks of section 3 at the start of section 2, \((w, b) = (-4, 2)\). Tags 3305 and 3363 are mature, and Tags 2193 and 3462 are immature. The model gives them a chance of being mature of 0.757, 0.987, 0.765 and 0.996. The probability it gives to the true answer is then 0.757, 0.987, \(1 - 0.765 = 0.235\) and \(1 - 0.996 = 0.004\). Taking \(-\ln\) of these gives 0.279, 0.014, 1.449 and 5.597, with a mean of \(L = 1.835\). Tag 3462 alone supplies 76% of the total. For all 268 sharks the mean at this start is 2.965. A few confident mistakes can supply most of the loss.

Symbols and derivations

\[ \ell_{\text{sq}} = (\hat{y} - y)^2 \qquad \frac{\partial \ell}{\partial \hat{y}} = 2\,(\hat{y} - y) \]

\[ \ell_{\text{CE}} = -\bigl[\,y\ln p + (1-y)\ln(1-p)\,\bigr],\quad p = \sigma(z) \qquad \frac{\partial \ell}{\partial z} = p - y \]

\[ \ell_{\text{CE}} = -\sum_{k=1}^{K} y_k \ln p_k = -\ln p_t,\quad p_k = \frac{e^{z_k}}{\sum_j e^{z_j}} \qquad \frac{\partial \ell}{\partial z_k} = p_k - y_k \qquad L = \frac{1}{m}\sum_{i=1}^{m}\ell_i \]

  • \(\hat{y}\) is a predicted number and \(y\) the true one. \(p\) is a probability and \(y\) a label, 0 or 1. \(z\) is the score, and \(t\) is the number of the true class.
  • With \(K\) classes, \(y_k\) is the one-hot label: 1 for the true class and 0 for the others (A3). Only the true class's term is left in the sum, which gives \(-\ln p_t\).
  • \(L\) is the average of the single-example losses over the \(m\) examples being used (A2). Mean squared error (MSE) is \(L\) for squared error.
Show the steps behind \(p_k - y_k\) for softmax

Write the loss with the logarithm of the sum: \(\ell = -\ln p_t = -\ln\dfrac{e^{z_t}}{\sum_j e^{z_j}} = -z_t + \ln\sum_j e^{z_j}\). Take the slope with respect to the score \(z_k\). The first term gives \(-1\) when \(k = t\) and 0 otherwise, which is \(-y_k\). The second term, by the chain rule (0.6), gives \(\dfrac{e^{z_k}}{\sum_j e^{z_j}} = p_k\). So \(\dfrac{\partial\ell}{\partial z_k} = p_k - y_k\).

For squared error through a sigmoid, \(\ell = (p - y)^2\) with \(p = \sigma(z)\). The chain rule gives \(2(p - y)\) times the slope of the sigmoid, \(p(1-p)\). The extra factor \(p(1-p)\) is the whole difference between the two pushes, apart from the constant 2.

Common mistakes

Debug tip. Check the loss at step 0. With \(K\) classes and a network that starts near a guess, cross-entropy should begin near \(\ln K\): 0.69 for two classes, 1.61 for five. A very different number can point to a bug in the labels or the loss, or to a confidently wrong start such as the one in section 2 (B8, after Karpathy's recipe). In PyTorch, nn.CrossEntropyLoss expects raw scores and applies the softmax itself, so applying softmax first gives a wrong, flatter loss.

In practice

In practice: use the library's combined function for softmax and cross-entropy. It works from the scores and avoids \(\ln 0\). Scale a target that is a number, as the weights in this chapter are scaled, so that its loss is easy to read. Averaging the loss over the batch, and not summing it, keeps the size of the gradient about the same when the batch size changes, so a learning rate that works at one batch size should work about as well at another.

In Python

import numpy as np

# 1. a number: Tag 3305 weighs 0.228 kg and the network says 0.300 kg
y_hat, y = 0.300, 0.228
print("squared error:", round((y_hat - y) ** 2, 4), " push 2(y_hat - y):", round(2 * (y_hat - y), 3))

# 2. two classes: Tag 4127 is a juvenile (y = 0) and the network's score is +5
z = 5.0
p = 1 / (1 + np.exp(-z))
print("cross-entropy:", round(-np.log(1 - p), 3), " squared error:", round(p ** 2, 3))
print("push, cross-entropy:", round(p, 3), " push, squared error:", round(2 * p * p * (1 - p), 3))

# 3. five species: made-up scores, true species is the hammerhead (index 3)
z = np.array([2.4, 1.2, 0.5, -0.4, -1.8])
p = np.exp(z - z.max()); p /= p.sum()                 # softmax
y = np.eye(5)[3]                                      # one-hot label
print("probabilities:", p.round(3))
print("cross-entropy:", round(-np.log(p[3]), 3))
print("push p - y:   ", (p - y).round(3), "sum:", round((p - y).sum(), 3) + 0.0)

push, cross-entropy: 0.993  push, squared error: 0.013
probabilities: [0.655 0.197 0.098 0.04  0.01 ]
cross-entropy: 3.223
push p - y:    [ 0.655  0.197  0.098 -0.96   0.01 ] sum: 0.0
import numpy as np

# four sharks of the made-up table: tags 3305, 3363, 2193, 3462 (length in cm; 1 = mature)
length = np.array([41.0, 34.2, 40.9, 31.4])
y = np.array([1, 1, 0, 0])
# scaled with the mean and spread of the 268 spadenose sharks
x = (length - 39.138) / 8.614

w, b = -4.0, 2.0                     # the confidently wrong start of section 2
p = 1 / (1 + np.exp(-(w * x + b)))   # chance of "mature"
p_true = np.where(y == 1, p, 1 - p)  # probability given to the true answer
loss = -np.log(p_true)
print("chance of mature:   ", p.round(3))
print("given to the truth: ", p_true.round(4))
print("loss per shark:     ", loss.round(3), " mean:", round(loss.mean(), 3))
print("product of the four:", f"{p_true.prod():.2e}")
print("-ln(product) / 4:   ", round(-np.log(p_true.prod()) / 4, 3))
chance of mature:    [0.757 0.987 0.765 0.996]
given to the truth:  [0.7568 0.9865 0.2347 0.0037]
loss per shark:      [0.279 0.014 1.449 5.597]  mean: 1.835
product of the four: 6.50e-04
-ln(product) / 4:    1.835

Why cross-entropy for probabilities

The last line of this printout shows how cross-entropy connects to likelihood. If the four sharks are treated as independent, the product of the four probabilities, 0.00065, is the chance that the model gave to all four true answers together. The mean of \(-\ln\) is \(-\ln(0.00065)/4 = 1.835\), the same number. So minimising the mean cross-entropy makes the labels in the table as likely as possible under the model (with that independence assumption), the idea of 0.7.

Where this is used

Used in: the push \(p - y\) is the number that backpropagation starts from (B4). Cross-entropy over a vocabulary is the loss that trains language models (D3). The next section (section 2) shows the same difference between the two losses as a walk across a landscape.

More questions

The scores of a three-class network give probabilities (0.7, 0.2, 0.1) and the true class is the second. What are the three pushes?

\(p - y = (0.7 - 0,\; 0.2 - 1,\; 0.1 - 0) = (0.7, -0.8, 0.1)\). They add up to 0, and the true class has the only negative push.

A two-class network shows a loss of 3.0 at step 0. What does \(\ln 2\) tell you, and what could explain 3.0?

A network that guesses gives \(\ln 2 = 0.69\). A loss of 3.0 means the network starts out confidently wrong, as the start \((-4, 2)\) of section 2 does (2.965). Check the labels, the loss function and the starting weights.

The loss landscape

Guess first. Any pair of a weight \(w\) and a bias \(b\) gives a model a loss, which we can draw as a height above the \((w, b)\) plane. If gradient descent starts where the model is confidently wrong, does the path reach the valley quickly or slowly, and does the loss matter?

That height is the loss landscape: valleys are low regions, and a plateau is a wide flat region. A step of gradient descent moves \((w, b)\) downhill by the learning rate \(\eta\) times the gradient, the slopes of the average loss \(L\) on \(w\) and \(b\). On a plateau the gradient is almost 0, so the steps are short. Here the model is a sigmoid neuron, which gives the probability that a shark is mature as \(p = \sigma(wx + b)\). In this formula \(x\) is the shark's length scaled to mean 0 and spread 1, \(w\) is the weight and \(b\) the bias. With cross-entropy the landscape slopes into the valley from all three starts, but with squared error the path from a confidently wrong start is slow on a plateau at \(\eta = 0.5\).

  1. Teal (cross-entropy, left) and coral (squared error, right) are the paths from the open circle, \((-4, 2)\), at \(\eta = 0.5\). Press "Run 300 steps": cross-entropy classifies 90.3% of the sharks correctly. Squared error is at 67.5%: its path has reached weights where the model calls all the sharks mature, and 67.5% of the sharks are mature.
  2. Set \(\eta\) to 3 and run again: squared error leaves the plateau after about 70 steps instead of 410.

From (−4, 2), cross-entropy has 90.3% of the sharks classified correctly after 50 steps, while squared error has 59.7% and then stays at 67.5% from step 85 to 408.

How it works

Take the first step from the start \((-4, 2)\) at \(\eta = 0.5\). For cross-entropy the gradient \((\partial L/\partial w,\ \partial L/\partial b)\) is \((-0.682, -0.004)\), so \(w\) moves to \(-3.659\). For squared error it is \((-0.050, -0.062)\), whose length is 8.5 times smaller, and \(w\) moves only to \(-3.975\). The gradient on \(w\) is the average of one term per shark: \((p - y)\,x\) for cross-entropy and \(2(p - y)\,p(1-p)\,x\) for squared error. Here \(y\) is 1 for a mature shark and 0 for an immature one. For Tag 3462, an immature shark to which the model gives probability 0.996 of "mature", the term is \(-0.895\) for cross-entropy but only \(-0.0066\) for squared error.

−3.659new \(w\), cross-entropy=−4current \(w\)−0.5learning rate \(\eta\)×−0.682\(\partial L/\partial w\)|−3.975squared error=−4−0.5×−0.050

Common belief. Gradient descent reaches the bottom quickly, as a ball rolls down a bowl.

Why it fails. In this example, squared error through a sigmoid has a plateau because the term of a single shark contains the factor \(p(1-p)\). This factor is the slope of the sigmoid, and at the start it is below 0.1 for 68% of the sharks.

Better account. The landscape depends on the loss, the model and the data, and cross-entropy keeps a steep slope while the model is confidently wrong. A larger \(\eta\) shortens the slow stretch, but too large an \(\eta\) makes the path bounce from side to side (Go deeper gives the limit).

  1. A network with a hidden unit can have several valleys. This one is \(f(x) = w_2 \tanh(w_1 x)\). The scaled length \(x\) is multiplied by \(w_1\), passed through \(\tanh\), which rises smoothly from −1 to 1, and multiplied by \(w_2\). The map shows the squared error between the output and the shark's body weight in kg, scaled in the same way, averaged over the 268 sharks. Press "Run 700 steps" from the start (1.5, 2), then choose the start (−1.5, 2) and run again.
  2. At \(\eta = 0.1\) the runs end near (0.38, 2.70) and (−0.39, −2.67), in two valleys with the same curve and the same loss after 700 steps, 0.119. This loss is still falling slowly. The two valleys are images of one another under \((w_1, w_2) \to (-w_1, -w_2)\), because \(\tanh(-u) = -\tanh(u)\) gives \((-w_1, -w_2)\) the same output as \((w_1, w_2)\). Different weights can give the same curve, so comparing the weights of two training runs does not show whether the networks differ.
  3. Choose the start (0, 0): the path does not move, because the gradient there is 0. A point with gradient 0 where the surface curves up in some directions and down in others is a saddle.

Quick quiz

At a point the gradient is \((-0.5, 0.2)\) and \(\eta = 0.1\). Where does the next step go, starting from \((1, 1)\)?

\((1, 1) - 0.1 \times (-0.5, 0.2) = (1.05, 0.98)\). The point moves to the right and slightly down.

Why is squared error with a sigmoid output slow from a confidently wrong start, and what fixes it?

Its gradient has the factor \(p(1-p)\), which is near 0 when the network is sure of its answer, so the step is tiny. Cross-entropy cancels that factor and keeps a slope there. A larger \(\eta\) also helps but needs tuning.

The numbers of the figure

From the start (−4, 2) at \(\eta = 0.5\), cross-entropy has a loss of 0.28 after 50 steps and calls 90% of the sharks right (0.282 and 90.3% to three digits). Squared error is then at 0.38 and 60% (0.382 and 59.7%). It stays at the always-adult answer, 67.5%, from step 85 to step 408, about 320 steps on the plateau. It leaves the plateau near step 414, where the share called right first exceeds 70%.

Reading the map

The model is \(p = \sigma(w x + b)\), one sigmoid neuron on the 268 spadenose sharks of A3. With only two weights, the whole landscape fits on one screen. Here \(x\) is the length scaled to a mean of 0 and a spread of 1, and the label is 1 for a mature shark. A shark is classified correctly (the readout says "right") when the model gives \(p\) above 0.5 to a mature shark or below 0.5 to an immature one. At the start, \(w = -4\) makes longer sharks less likely to be mature, which is backwards. A map shows the loss for all pairs \((w, b)\) in its range: the darker the shade, the higher the loss, and the thin lines are contour lines, curves along which the loss is the same (0.6). The open circle is the start. The \(\times\) is the valley floor, at \(w \approx 4.6\) and \(b \approx 2.5\). It is the best sigmoid of A3, with a steepness of 0.535 per cm and a midpoint of 34.5 cm, written in scaled units. Press "Run 300 steps" and watch the two paths. A step points along the negative gradient, which is perpendicular to the contour line through that point, because the gradient points straight uphill (0.6). The two axes of the map have different scales, so on the screen the angles do not look like right angles. Click either map to choose a new start, or switch to the 3D view and rotate the surface.

Why the two gradients differ

The gradients of the first step both lead downhill, but they differ: the squared error one is shorter and points in another direction. The reason is the factor \(p(1-p)\), which multiplies the term of a single shark in the gradient. At this start the model gives almost all juveniles a probability near 1 and about a third of the adults a probability below 0.2. In the data, \(p(1-p)\) is below 0.1 for 68% of the sharks, about two in three. For cross-entropy the first step moves \(w\) from \(-4\) to \(-4 - 0.5 \times (-0.682) = -3.659\) and \(b\) from 2 to 2.002. On the plateau, between steps 100 and 300, the model calls all the sharks mature and \(p(1-p)\) is below 0.1 for 90% to 100% of them. The gradient size of squared error shown in the readout falls from 0.080 at step 0 to between 0.008 and 0.013 at steps 150 to 300.

Tag 3462 shows the factor at work. It is immature, with a scaled length of \(-0.898\), and the model gives it \(p = 0.996\). Its term in the cross-entropy gradient on \(w\) is \((p - y)\,x = 0.996 \times (-0.898) = -0.895\). Its term in the squared error gradient is \(2\,(p - y)\,p(1-p)\,x = 2 \times 0.996 \times 0.0037 \times (-0.898) = -0.0066\), about 135 times smaller. The cross-entropy loss of this shark is 5.597, a big mistake, but its term in the squared error gradient is tiny.

The second step

The second step starts at \((-3.659, 2.002)\). The new cross-entropy gradient is \((-0.671, 0.008)\), so the weight moves to \(-3.659 + 0.5 \times 0.671 = -3.323\) and the bias to 1.998. The loss falls from 2.965 to 2.735 after the first step and to 2.511 after the second. Squared error falls from 0.568 to 0.565 and then to 0.562. The cross-entropy steps are about 0.34 long, and the squared error steps about 0.04 long, the length of the gradient times \(\eta\).

Symbols

\[ \frac{\partial L_{\text{CE}}}{\partial w} = \frac{1}{m}\sum_{i=1}^{m}(p_i - y_i)\,x_i \qquad \frac{\partial L_{\text{sq}}}{\partial w} = \frac{1}{m}\sum_{i=1}^{m}2\,(p_i - y_i)\,p_i(1 - p_i)\,x_i \qquad \begin{pmatrix} w \\ b \end{pmatrix} \leftarrow \begin{pmatrix} w \\ b \end{pmatrix} - \eta\,\nabla L \]

  • \(p_i = \sigma(w x_i + b)\) is the model's probability for shark \(i\), \(y_i\) its label and \(x_i\) its scaled length. The bias slopes are the same sums with \(x_i\) left out. The first formula is derived in A3.
  • \(\nabla L\) is the vector of the two slopes (0.6). The step is \(\eta\) times its length, so a short gradient gives a short step.
  • Near the valley floor the two losses agree: their valleys are at almost the same place, \(w = 4.61\) and \(4.64\). They differ in the approach.

Try this

Try this. (1) Run the three starts and say which loss reaches the valley first. (2) Set \(\eta\) to 3 and run again from the first start. (3) Click the squared error map on the plateau, at \((-1, 3)\), and run.

Check your predictions

(1) Cross-entropy calls 90% of the sharks right first from the two far starts. From (−3, −3), squared error calls most sharks juveniles for 100 steps (32.5% right at step 100), and cross-entropy has 89.9% right at step 50. From (2, 0), close to the valley, both reach 90% right in under 100 steps. (2) A big \(\eta\) helps squared error most: at \(\eta = 3\) it leaves the plateau by step 100, and cross-entropy has 90% of the sharks right after 10 steps. In this example a rate that is right for one loss is too small for the other, so the learning rate has to be tuned for the loss in use. (3) A start on the plateau has a gradient near 0, so the path crawls for about 100 steps before the slope picks up.

In practice

In practice: you cannot draw this picture for a full-size network, which has millions of weights. You see the loss curve, and you check it against what you know. A flat start is a warning sign: it may be a plateau, a dead unit, or a learning rate that is too small. Starting weights are random numbers, so that units do not start identical, and their spread is chosen to keep the size of signals and slopes useful (B6). Li and colleagues (2018) drew two-dimensional slices through the loss of neural networks to compare landscapes.

Why the walk slows near the valley floor

Why does the walk slow down near the valley floor? Near a minimum the loss along one direction looks like \(\tfrac{1}{2}k\,(w - w^{*})^{2}\), where \(k\) is the curvature (0.6) and \(w^{*}\) is the floor. A gradient step gives \(w - \eta k\,(w - w^{*})\), so the gap to the floor is multiplied by \(1 - \eta k\). Take a gap of 3 and \(k = 1\). With \(\eta = 0.5\) the gaps are 3, 1.5, 0.75, 0.375. With \(\eta = 1.5\) they are 3, \(-1.5\), 0.75, \(-0.375\): the path bounces and still shrinks. With \(\eta = 2.5\) they are 3, \(-4.5\), 6.75, \(-10.1\), and the path blows up. So \(\eta\) must stay below \(2/k\).

The cross-entropy of this chapter's neuron has a steep direction and a flat one. At the valley floor the table of curvatures has the values 0.0914 and 0.0072, as the printout below shows. Near the floor the largest safe \(\eta\) is \(2/0.0914 = 22\). With \(\eta = 0.5\) the flat direction shrinks its gap by \(1 - 0.5 \times 0.0072 = 0.9964\) per step, a time constant of about 280 steps. That is why the last stretch to the floor is slow, and why a larger \(\eta\) helps here. To choose \(\eta\) on a new problem, try 0.001, 0.01, 0.1 and 1 for 100 steps apiece and keep the largest one whose loss still falls steadily.

In Python

import numpy as np, pandas as pd

d = pd.read_csv("catch.csv")
d = d[d.species == "spadenose"]  # the 268 spadenose sharks (made up)
x = ((d.length_cm - d.length_cm.mean()) / d.length_cm.std(ddof=0)).to_numpy()
y = d.mature.to_numpy().astype(float)

def gradients(w, b):
    p = 1 / (1 + np.exp(-(w * x + b)))
    ce = np.array([np.mean((p - y) * x), np.mean(p - y)])
    sq = 2 * (p - y) * p * (1 - p)  # squared error has the extra factor p (1 - p)
    return ce, np.array([np.mean(sq * x), np.mean(sq)])

for name, which in (("cross-entropy", 0), ("squared error", 1)):
    w, b = -4.0, 2.0
    print(name)
    for step in range(1, 4):
        g = gradients(w, b)[which]
        w, b = w - 0.5 * g[0], b - 0.5 * g[1]
        print(f"  step {step}: gradient ({g[0]:.3f}, {g[1]:.3f}) -> (w, b) = ({w:.3f}, {b:.3f})")

p = 1 / (1 + np.exp(-(4.61 * x + 2.48)))  # the valley floor of the cross-entropy
f = p * (1 - p)
# the table of curvatures (second slopes) of the loss
H = np.array([[np.mean(f * x * x), np.mean(f * x)], [np.mean(f * x), np.mean(f)]])
print("curvatures at the valley floor:", np.linalg.eigvalsh(H).round(4))

  step 3: gradient (-0.659, 0.022) -> (w, b) = (-2.994, 1.987)

  step 1: gradient (-0.050, -0.062) -> (w, b) = (-3.975, 2.031)

A network's landscape has more than one valley

A single sigmoid neuron with cross-entropy has one valley. A network with a hidden unit can have more. Take the smallest network that bends: one input \(x\), one tanh hidden unit and one output, \(f(x) = w_2 \tanh(w_1 x)\), with no biases. Here it predicts the scaled weight of a spadenose shark from its scaled length, with squared error. The second map above has \(w_1\) across and \(w_2\) up.

At the default \(\eta = 0.1\) the two valleys are mirror images. After 700 steps the run from (1.5, 2) ends near (0.38, 2.70) and the run from (−1.5, 2) near (−0.39, −2.67). Both give the same curve and a loss of 0.119, and the loss keeps falling very slowly along the valley. At (0, 0) the gradient is 0, but the point is a saddle and no valley.

Press "Run 700 steps" from the starts one by one. The start at (1.5, 2) goes to the upper right valley and (−1.5, 2) crosses to the lower left one. The two end at different weights, with the same curve and the same loss. The reason is that \(\tanh\) is an odd function, so flipping the sign of both weights gives the same output. The valleys are long and curved because the product \(w_1 w_2\) is what mostly sets the slope of the curve, and many pairs have the same product. The start at (0, 0) does not move at all. The reason is in the gradient:

\[ \frac{\partial \ell}{\partial w_2} = 2\,(f - t)\,\tanh(w_1 x) \qquad \frac{\partial \ell}{\partial w_1} = 2\,(f - t)\,w_2\,\bigl(1 - \tanh^2(w_1 x)\bigr)\,x \]

  • \(t\) is the target (the scaled weight) and \(f = w_2 \tanh(w_1 x)\) the network's output. The second slope uses the chain rule through the tanh (0.6).
  • At \(w_1 = 0\) the factor \(\tanh(w_1 x)\) is 0, so the first slope is 0. At \(w_2 = 0\) the factor \(w_2\) is 0, so the second slope is 0. At the origin both vanish.

This has two consequences. A bad start can be a stuck start: all weights at 0 is the classic example (B6). And weights are not unique. Networks trained from different starts can have different weights and the same function. So comparing the weights of two training runs is not a safe way to compare the networks. At a learning rate of 0.3 or more, this narrow valley makes the path bounce from side to side and stay at a higher loss, the \(\eta < 2/k\) limit of 0.6. Near the end of the \(\eta = 0.1\) run the largest curvature across the valley is about 8.6, so \(\eta\) must stay below \(2/8.6 = 0.23\).

Here are the two slopes for one shark. Tag 3305 has a scaled length of 0.216 and a scaled weight of 0.016. At \((w_1, w_2) = (1.5, 2)\) the hidden value is \(\tanh(1.5 \times 0.216) = 0.313\), and the output is \(f = 2 \times 0.313 = 0.627\). The error is \(f - t = 0.611\), so \(2\,(f - t) = 1.222\). The slope on \(w_2\) is \(1.222 \times 0.313 = 0.383\). The slope on \(w_1\) is \(1.222 \times 2 \times (1 - 0.313^2) \times 0.216 = 0.477\). Both are positive, so on this shark's evidence gradient descent lowers both weights, since the network predicts too heavy a shark. Over all 268 sharks the slopes at this point are 0.510 and 0.924.

The saddle is not a trap for starts near it. On this map the gradient is 0 only at the origin itself. At \(\eta = 0.3\) a start at \((0.01, 0.01)\) leaves it and reaches a loss under 0.2 in 14 steps, while a start at \((0, 0)\) stays for ever. The gradient is small near the saddle and grows as the walk moves away, so the walk speeds up as it leaves.

In Python (the one-hidden-unit network)

import numpy as np, pandas as pd

d = pd.read_csv("catch.csv")
d = d[d.species == "spadenose"]
x = ((d.length_cm - d.length_cm.mean()) / d.length_cm.std(ddof=0)).to_numpy()
kg = d.weight_kg
t = ((kg - kg.mean()) / kg.std(ddof=0)).to_numpy()  # scaled weight

def loss_and_grad(w1, w2, x, t):  # f(x) = w2 * tanh(w1 * x), squared error
    th = np.tanh(w1 * x)
    e = 2 * (w2 * th - t)
    slopes = np.array([np.mean(e * w2 * (1 - th ** 2) * x), np.mean(e * th)])
    return np.mean((w2 * th - t) ** 2), slopes

i = (d.record_id == 3305).to_numpy()  # one shark: Tag 3305
l, g = loss_and_grad(1.5, 2.0, x[i], t[i])
print("Tag 3305 at (1.5, 2): squared error", round(l, 3), " slopes", g.round(3))
print("all 268 sharks:       slopes", loss_and_grad(1.5, 2.0, x, t)[1].round(3))

# on the saddle, next to it, and the start of the figure
for start in [(0.0, 0.0), (0.01, 0.01), (1.5, 2.0)]:
    w1, w2 = start
    for step in range(1, 401):
        g = loss_and_grad(w1, w2, x, t)[1]
        w1, w2 = w1 - 0.3 * g[0], w2 - 0.3 * g[1]
        if loss_and_grad(w1, w2, x, t)[0] < 0.2:
            break
    final = loss_and_grad(w1, w2, x, t)[0]
    print(f"start {start}: loss {final:.3f} after {step} steps, at ({w1:.2f}, {w2:.2f})")

all 268 sharks:       slopes [0.51  0.924]
start (0.0, 0.0): loss 1.000 after 400 steps, at (0.00, 0.00)
start (0.01, 0.01): loss 0.191 after 14 steps, at (0.92, 1.20)

Common mistakes

Debug tip. If the loss does not move from step 0 and the gradient norm is 0, look for weights that are all 0, or a dead ReLU layer. If the loss falls and then rises or oscillates, lower the learning rate. Print the gradient norm along with the loss.

More questions

A weight is 2 away from the floor, where the curvature is \(k = 0.5\). Where is the gap after one step with \(\eta = 1.5\), and with \(\eta = 5\)?

The gap is multiplied by \(1 - \eta k\). For \(\eta = 1.5\) the factor is \(1 - 0.75 = 0.25\), so the gap becomes 0.5. For \(\eta = 5\) the factor is \(1 - 2.5 = -1.5\), so the gap becomes \(-3\): the weight jumps past the floor and ends farther away. The limit is \(2/k = 4\).

Batches and epochs

Guess first. A step can use the gradient from all 268 spadenose sharks in the table, or from only 16 of them. With 16 per step, how many steps does one pass through the table take, and is the gradient from 16 sharks the same as the one from 268?

A mini-batch is a small random group of \(B\) examples (here sharks). A step is one update of the weights, made with the average gradient of the batch. An epoch is one pass through all \(m\) examples, so it takes \(\lceil m/B \rceil\) steps (rounded up). Usually the training program shuffles the examples, putting them in a new random order, at the start of an epoch. A batch gradient usually differs from the gradient over all \(m\) examples, but the average over all possible random batches equals it.

  1. A square is a shark, coral if mature and navy if not. With \(B = 16\), press "One step": the 16 outlined squares are the batch, 63% mature against 67.5% in the table.
  2. Press "One step" 16 more times, or "Play". In the first epoch the share of mature sharks in a batch runs from 50% to 81%, and the last batch has 12 sharks.
  3. Drag \(B\) to 268 or to 1 and read the steps in an epoch.
17steps per epoch \(\lceil m/B \rceil\)=⌈268sharks \(m\)÷16batch size \(B\)⌉
Epoch: 1Step: 0 of 17Updates so far: 0Sharks in this batch: 0Mature in this batch: none yet

An epoch of 268 sharks takes 17 steps with \(B = 16\), 1 step with \(B = 268\) and 268 steps with \(B = 1\).

How it works

Take Tags 3305, 3363, 2193 and 3462 and the sigmoid neuron of the last section at \((w, b) = (-4, 2)\). Their cross-entropy slopes on \(w\) are \(-0.053\), \(0.008\), \(0.157\) and \(-0.895\), so the batch gradient on \(w\) is their average, \(-0.196\). All 268 sharks give the full gradient \((-0.682, -0.004)\). The batch gradient on \(w\) has the same sign as the full gradient. On \(b\) the four slopes are \(-0.243\), \(-0.013\), 0.765 and 0.996, so their average, the batch gradient, is 0.376, where the full gradient has \(-0.004\). The gap between a batch gradient and the full gradient is called noise.

−3.902new \(w\)=−4current \(w\)−0.5learning rate \(\eta\)×−0.196average of the 4 slopes

With \(m = 268\) and \(B = 16\), \(268/16 = 16.75\), so an epoch takes \(\lceil 268/16 \rceil = 17\) steps: 16 batches of 16 sharks and a last batch of \(268 - 256 = 12\). After \(E\) epochs the weights have been updated \(E\lceil m/B \rceil\) times.

Common belief. A step must use all the data, or the gradient is wrong.

Why it fails. The gradient of the average loss is the average of the gradients of single examples. If one example is drawn at random, its gradient averages to the full gradient over all possible draws, and so does the mean of \(B\) drawn gradients. So one batch is noisy but correct on average. The 17 steps of an epoch cost 268 gradients, the same as one step on all sharks.

Better account. Mini-batches trade accuracy per step for more steps: a batch gradient is cheap and approximate.

Quick quiz

The table has 600 records and the batch size is 128. How many steps is an epoch, and how large is the last batch?

\(\lceil 600/128 \rceil = 5\) steps. The first four batches use 512 records, so the last batch has \(600 - 512 = 88\).

Why is the mini-batch gradient correct on average, though wrong for one batch?

An example's gradient is drawn from the table at random, and the average of the loss over the table is the average of the examples' losses. The average of many random batches is the full gradient, but one batch scatters around it.

Go deeper the four sharks, Python, why shuffle, symbols about 5 min

Reading the figure

A square is a shark, coral if it is mature and navy if not. The squares are laid out in the shuffled order for this epoch. Press "One step" or "Play". The outlined squares are the batch for this step, and the faded squares have been used. Move the batch size and see the counts change. When the last batch has run, the epoch ends, the sharks are shuffled again, and the next epoch starts. Notice the share of mature sharks in the outlined batch. In the whole table it is 67.5%. A batch of 4 may be 25% or 100% mature, and a batch of 128 is usually within a few points of 67.5%. That spread is where the noise of the next section comes from.

The four sharks in detail

Here is one batch with numbers. Take the model at \((w, b) = (-4, 2)\) and four sharks: Tag 3305 (41.0 cm, mature), Tag 3363 (34.2 cm, mature), Tag 2193 (40.9 cm, immature) and Tag 3462 (31.4 cm, immature). Their scaled lengths are 0.216, \(-0.573\), 0.205 and \(-0.898\). The model gives them \(p = 0.757, 0.987, 0.765, 0.996\), so \(p - y = -0.243, -0.013, 0.765, 0.996\). Multiply these by the lengths to get \(-0.053, 0.008, 0.157, -0.895\). The batch gradient on \(w\) is their average, \(-0.196\), and on \(b\) it is the average of the \(p - y\), \(0.376\). The gradient from all 268 sharks is \((-0.682, -0.004)\). The four sharks give the same sign for \(w\), but their gradient on \(b\) is 0.376 where all 268 sharks give \(-0.004\): that difference is noise.

Why the batch gradient is right on average

Why is the batch gradient right on average? Draw one shark at random from the 268, with probability 1/268 for any given shark. The expected value of its gradient is \(\tfrac{1}{268}\sum_i g_i\), the full gradient. A batch of \(B\) is the average of \(B\) such draws, and an average of values that all have this expected value has it too. So the batch gradient is right on average: it is an unbiased estimate of the full gradient. The next printout draws five batches of 16 from one shuffle. Their gradients on \(w\) are \(-1.07, -0.73, -0.58, -0.62, -0.46\), with a mean of \(-0.69\), against \(-0.68\) for all 268. The bias gradients run from \(-0.10\) to \(0.30\), and the batch with 50% mature sharks has the largest. That is the noise of the next section. Shuffling again at the start of an epoch changes which sharks share a batch. The noise then differs from one epoch to the next, and the path does not repeat one zigzag.

In Python

import numpy as np, pandas as pd

d = pd.read_csv("catch.csv")
d = d[d.species == "spadenose"]
x = ((d.length_cm - d.length_cm.mean()) / d.length_cm.std(ddof=0)).to_numpy()
y = d.mature.to_numpy().astype(float)
w, b = -4.0, 2.0  # the confidently wrong start

def gradient(idx):
    p = 1 / (1 + np.exp(-(w * x[idx] + b)))
    return np.array([np.mean((p - y[idx]) * x[idx]), np.mean(p - y[idx])])

print("all 268:         ", gradient(np.arange(len(x))).round(3))
order = np.random.default_rng(0).permutation(len(x))  # one shuffle
for k in range(5):
    idx = order[16 * k: 16 * (k + 1)]
    print(f"batch {k + 1} of 16:    ", gradient(idx).round(3), " mature share", y[idx].mean())

by_length = np.argsort(x)  # the table sorted from short to long
print("mature share of the shortest 16 sharks:", y[by_length[:16]].mean())
print("mature share of the longest 16 sharks: ", y[by_length[-16:]].mean())

Why shuffle

The last line of the printout explains the advice to shuffle. In a table sorted by length, the first 16 sharks are all immature and the last 16 are all mature. Taken in order, the first batches would push the model to call all the sharks immature, and the last batches would push it back.

Symbols

\[ \theta \leftarrow \theta - \eta\,\frac{1}{|\mathcal{B}|}\sum_{i\in\mathcal{B}} \nabla \ell_i(\theta) \qquad \text{steps per epoch} = \left\lceil \frac{m}{B}\right\rceil \qquad \text{updates after } E \text{ epochs} = E\left\lceil \frac{m}{B}\right\rceil \]

  • \(\theta\) means all the weights (here \(w\) and \(b\)). \(\mathcal{B}\) is the set of examples in the current batch and \(|\mathcal{B}|\) its size, which is \(B\) except for a short last batch.
  • \(\nabla \ell_i\) is the gradient of the loss for example \(i\). The batch gradient is their average, an estimate of the gradient over all \(m\) examples.
  • \(\lceil\cdot\rceil\) rounds up. For \(B = 20\): \(\lceil 268/20 \rceil = 14\) steps, 13 full batches of 20 and a last batch of 8. After 30 epochs that is 420 updates. For \(B = 64\): 5 steps, with a last batch of 12.

Common mistakes

Debug tip. Shuffle. If the table is sorted, for example by species or by length, the batches contain mostly one kind of shark and the gradient jumps from step to step. Shuffle at the start of an epoch, and make sure that labels and inputs are shuffled together. A last batch that is smaller than the others is normal. A batch of size 1 can make some losses and normalisation layers fail.

In practice

In practice: typical batch sizes for networks are 16 to 256, limited by memory on the graphics card. Photos take much more memory than rows of a table, so a batch of photos is often smaller. Report progress in epochs, since one epoch is the same amount of data for all batch sizes. With \(B = 100\) an epoch is 3 steps, of 100, 100 and 68 sharks. Some libraries can drop the short last batch, and some losses need it kept.

More questions

A table sorted by length is used in order, with \(B = 16\) and no shuffling. What goes wrong in the first few batches?

The shortest sharks are all immature, so the first batches contain no mature shark. Their gradient pushes the model to call all the sharks immature. Later batches, with the longest sharks, push the other way. The path swings, and the end of an epoch is wherever the last batches left it.

Noisy steps

Guess first. You train with batch size 1 and with batch size 268 for the same 10 epochs at the same learning rate. Which path is smoother, and which one gets to the valley first?

The gradient of a mini-batch is the gradient of the full batch (all \(m\) examples) plus noise, the gap between the two. If the gradients of single examples have spread \(\sigma\) (standard deviation), the noise of a batch of \(B\) examples has spread about \(\sigma/\sqrt{B}\). A small batch takes many noisy steps per epoch, and a large batch takes few steady ones. In this example, at \(\eta = 0.3\) and 10 epochs, \(B = 16\) reaches a lower loss than \(B = 268\), because it takes 170 steps against 10. Gradient descent with mini-batches is called stochastic gradient descent (SGD), and the full batch has no noise.

  1. Drag \(B\) from 16 to 268: the readout changes from 170 steps and a final loss of 0.250 to 10 steps and 1.717. Coral dots on the teal path mark the ends of epochs.
  2. Drag \(B\) to 1: the path becomes a zigzag of 2,680 steps with a final loss of 0.233, and "Another shuffle" changes the path and the final loss.
  3. The boxes under the plots compare \(\sigma/\sqrt{B}\) with the spread of 400 random batches: 0.037 and 0.040 at \(B = 16\).

The path from the start (−4, 2); coral dots mark the ends of epochs

Loss for five batch sizes; the chosen one is thick

The noise of the gradient on \(w\) at the valley floor, from 400 random batches at eight sizes (dots) and by formula (dashed)

0spread for \(B = 1\), \(\sigma\)÷0\(\sqrt{B}\) for \(B\) = 0≈0formulavs sampled0spread of batches
Steps per epoch: 0Steps in all: 0Loss at the end: 0

After 10 epochs at \(\eta = 0.3\), \(B = 16\) has taken 170 steps and reached a loss of 0.250, near the lowest possible 0.232; \(B = 268\) has taken 10 steps and is at 1.717.

How it works

At the valley floor, the lowest point, the slopes of the sharks' losses on \(w\) have spread \(\sigma = 0.153\). For a batch of \(B = 16\) the equation below gives a spread of 0.037. At \(\eta = 0.3\) a step turns this noise into a random change of \(w\), a jitter, of about \(0.3 \times 0.037 = 0.011\), against \(0.3 \times 0.153 = 0.046\) for \(B = 1\).

\(\sigma\)spread of a single shark: 0.153÷\(\sqrt{B}\)4 for \(B = 16\)×\(\sqrt{\tfrac{m-B}{m-1}}\)correction: 0.972=0.037batch gradient spread

The \(B\) slopes have variance \(\sigma^2\), the square of the spread. For independent draws, where one draw does not change the chances of the next, variances add, so the sum has variance \(B\sigma^2\) and spread \(\sigma\sqrt{B}\). Dividing the sum by \(B\) divides its spread by \(B\), which leaves \(\sigma\sqrt{B}/B = \sigma/\sqrt{B}\). Drawing without putting back makes the batch resemble the table more closely, so the spread is a little smaller. The correction for this, the last factor of the equation, is near 1 for small \(B\) and 0 for \(B = m\). The training loop is in Go deeper.

Common belief. A bigger batch is always better, because its gradient is more accurate.

Why it fails. A more accurate gradient costs more per step and gives fewer steps per epoch. The full-batch run is still far from the valley floor after 10 epochs because it has taken only 10 steps, while \(B = 16\) is near it after 170.

Better account. The batch size sets a trade-off between noisy, cheap steps and steady, costly ones, and a good learning rate depends on it.

Quick quiz

The noise of a batch gradient is 0.15 at \(B = 1\). Roughly what is it at \(B = 25\), and at \(B = 100\)?

\(0.15/\sqrt{25} = 0.03\) and \(0.15/\sqrt{100} = 0.015\). To halve the noise again, the batch has to grow by a factor of 4.

At \(\eta = 0.3\) the weight jitters by 0.011 per step with \(B = 16\). How can you halve the jitter, and what does it cost?

Make the batch 4 times larger, \(B = 64\), since the noise falls like \(1/\sqrt{B}\). That costs 4 times the gradients per step. Or halve \(\eta\) to 0.15. That costs speed, since all the steps are half as long.

Go deeper noise formula, Python loop, symbols, batch size about 7 min

Reading the figure

Slide the batch size from 268 down to 1. At 268 the path is a short smooth curve with only 10 dots after the start, one per epoch. It has covered less than a quarter of the way from the start to the valley floor. At 16 the path is a rough line of 170 steps that reaches the valley. At 1 the path is a jagged zigzag of 2,680 steps that jitters around the valley floor, because a single shark pushes the weights hard in its own direction. The noise dots in the lower plot stop at \(B = 128\), since for \(B = 268\) the batch is the whole table and the noise is 0. Now switch the loss plot to "against steps". The curves for the five batch sizes then lie close to one falling line: a step with 268 sharks lowers the loss about as much as a step with 16. But a step with 268 sharks costs 268 gradients, and a step with 16 costs 16. So the fair comparison counts the gradients, which is the comparison per epoch that the first view shows, and in epochs the small batches win at \(\eta = 0.3\).

How the noise shrinks

The dots in the lower plot show how the noise shrinks. At the valley floor the average gradient is almost 0, but single sharks disagree: the spread of one shark's contribution is \(\sigma = 0.153\). The average of \(B\) sharks has spread \(\sigma/\sqrt{B}\), times a small correction that the formula below explains. The spread is 0.076 for 4 sharks, 0.037 for 16 and 0.017 for 64. Without the correction the last two would read 0.038 and 0.019. Quadrupling the batch halves the noise. The calculation under "How it works" shows why: the average of \(B\) independent values has variance \(\sigma^2/B\). This is the standard error of 0.7.

Symbols

\[ \operatorname{Var}\!\Bigl(\frac{1}{B}\sum_{j=1}^{B} g_j\Bigr) = \frac{\sigma^{2}}{B} \qquad \text{spread of the batch gradient} \approx \frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{B}}\sqrt{\frac{m - B}{m - 1}} \]

  • \(g_j\) is the gradient contribution of one example, here \((p_j - y_j)\,x_j\) for the weight \(w\), and \(\sigma\) its spread over the table.
  • The second factor is a correction for drawing without putting back. It is close to 1 for small \(B\) and 0 for \(B = m\), where the batch is the whole table and there is no noise.
  • The formula assumes the draws are independent, which is nearly true when \(B\) is much smaller than \(m\). In the figure the dots follow the formula.

What the noise does to the path

What does this noise do to the path? A step is \(\eta\) times the gradient, so noise in the gradient becomes jitter in the weight. At the valley floor and \(\eta = 0.3\), a batch of 1 moves \(w\) by a random amount of about \(0.3 \times 0.153 = 0.046\) per step. A batch of 16 moves it by \(0.3 \times 0.037 = 0.011\). The B = 1 path jumps about four times as far around the floor as the B = 16 path. Its final loss can therefore vary more from one shuffle to the next. Lowering \(\eta\) late in training shrinks the jitter in proportion (B5). The printout draws 4000 random batches at four sizes and compares their spread with the formula.

In Python (the noise of the gradient)

import numpy as np, pandas as pd

d = pd.read_csv("catch.csv")
d = d[d.species == "spadenose"]
x = ((d.length_cm - d.length_cm.mean()) / d.length_cm.std(ddof=0)).to_numpy()
y = d.mature.to_numpy().astype(float)
m = len(x)

p = 1 / (1 + np.exp(-(4.61 * x + 2.48)))  # the model at the valley floor
g = (p - y) * x                           # the push of each shark on w
print(f"one shark: mean {g.mean():.4f}, spread {g.std():.3f}")

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
for B in (1, 4, 16, 64):
    batches = [g[rng.choice(m, B, replace=False)].mean() for _ in range(4000)]
    formula = g.std() / np.sqrt(B) * np.sqrt((m - B) / (m - 1))
    print(f"B = {B:2d}: spread of 4000 batches {np.std(batches):.3f}, formula {formula:.3f}, "
          f"jitter at eta 0.3: {0.3 * formula:.3f}")
one shark: mean -0.0001, spread 0.153
B =  1: spread of 4000 batches 0.152, formula 0.153, jitter at eta 0.3: 0.046
B =  4: spread of 4000 batches 0.074, formula 0.076, jitter at eta 0.3: 0.023
B = 16: spread of 4000 batches 0.037, formula 0.037, jitter at eta 0.3: 0.011
B = 64: spread of 4000 batches 0.017, formula 0.017, jitter at eta 0.3: 0.005

More on the batch size

In one study of image networks, batches of 2 to 32 gave the best test results (Masters and Luschi, 2018). Larger batches are still used when a graphics card runs them in parallel. Set \(B = 1\) and \(\eta = 1\) and press "Another shuffle" a few times. The path keeps jumping and the loss after 10 epochs changes from run to run, while \(B = 16\) at the same \(\eta\) stays near 0.233.

Common mistakes

Debug tip. A jagged training loss is normal with small batches, because a step uses a different group of sharks. Do not judge a run by the loss of one batch. Measure the loss on the full table at the end of an epoch, as the figure does, or on a fixed held-out set (A4). If the loss is jagged and not trending down at the same time, lower the learning rate.

In practice

In practice: start with a batch size of 32 for a small table and a learning rate near 0.01 to 0.1, then tune. A common mistake is to add the loss over the batch and not average it. The step is then \(B\) times larger, and a learning rate that worked for one batch size diverges for another. A second one is to compare two batch sizes after the same number of steps and not the same number of epochs. Bottou, Curtis and Nocedal (2018) review stochastic gradient methods for large problems.

In Python (the training loop)

import numpy as np

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
m = 268
length = rng.normal(39.1, 8.6, m)                     # made-up lengths, cm
x = (length - 39.1) / 8.6                             # scaled
y = (rng.uniform(size=m) < 1 / (1 + np.exp(-(4.6 * x + 2.5)))).astype(float)   # made-up labels: 1 = mature

def loss(w, b):
    p = 1 / (1 + np.exp(-(w * x + b)))
    return -np.mean(y * np.log(p) + (1 - y) * np.log(1 - p))

w, b, eta, B = -4.0, 2.0, 0.3, 16
print(f"start: loss {loss(w, b):.3f}")
for epoch in range(1, 11):
    order = rng.permutation(m)                         # shuffle again at the start of an epoch
    for start in range(0, m, B):
        idx = order[start:start + B]                   # one mini-batch (the last one may be smaller)
        p = 1 / (1 + np.exp(-(w * x[idx] + b)))
        w -= eta * np.mean((p - y[idx]) * x[idx])      # average gradient over the batch
        b -= eta * np.mean(p - y[idx])
    steps = epoch * int(np.ceil(m / B))
    print(f"epoch {epoch:2d}: {steps:3d} steps, loss {loss(w, b):.3f}, w = {w:.2f}, b = {b:.2f}")
start: loss 2.796
epoch  1:  17 steps, loss 1.098, w = -1.09, b = 1.82
epoch  2:  34 steps, loss 0.456, w = 0.62, b = 1.31
epoch  3:  51 steps, loss 0.339, w = 1.37, b = 1.20
epoch  4:  68 steps, loss 0.306, w = 1.77, b = 1.26
epoch  5:  85 steps, loss 0.290, w = 2.05, b = 1.34
epoch  6: 102 steps, loss 0.279, w = 2.27, b = 1.43
epoch  7: 119 steps, loss 0.272, w = 2.44, b = 1.52
epoch  8: 136 steps, loss 0.267, w = 2.56, b = 1.64
epoch  9: 153 steps, loss 0.262, w = 2.69, b = 1.71
epoch 10: 170 steps, loss 0.259, w = 2.81, b = 1.74

This is the whole loop of a network trainer: shuffle, cut into batches, compute the average gradient, step. Here the gradient is the one of A3. For a deeper network, backpropagation (B4) supplies the gradient and the loop stays the same. The labels here are made up from a formula, and the run starts at the same confident wrong place as the figure.

Where this is used

Used in: the optimisers of B5 change what is done with the batch gradient, for example by averaging it over steps. The debugging recipe of B8 starts with the loss at step 0 and an overfit of one small batch.

More questions

Run A uses \(B = 16\) for 10 epochs and run B uses \(B = 268\) for 10 epochs. Which has taken more steps, and which has used more data?

Run A has taken 170 steps and run B only 10. Both have used the same data: 10 passes over the 268 sharks. That is why epochs are the fair measure of work.

Exercises

Theory

  1. theory A sigmoid output gives \(p = 0.9\) to a juvenile shark (\(y = 0\)). Compute the cross-entropy loss, the squared error loss, and the two pushes on the score \(z\). How many times larger is the first push?

    Hint

    Cross-entropy for \(y = 0\) is \(-\ln(1 - p)\), with push \(p - y\). Squared error has push \(2(p - y)\,p\,(1 - p)\).

  2. theory A four-class network gives the probabilities (0.1, 0.6, 0.2, 0.1) and the true class is the third. Find the cross-entropy loss and the four pushes \(p_k - y_k\). Check that they add up to 0, and explain in a sentence why they must.

  3. theory The table has \(m = 1000\) examples and the batch size is 48. How many steps are in an epoch? How many examples are in the last batch? How many updates happen in 20 epochs?

  4. theory The spread of a single example's gradient is 0.4. Find the spread of a batch gradient for \(B = 4, 16, 100\), ignoring the correction for drawing without putting back. Then show that, if all batches have the same size, the average of the batch gradients over one epoch is the gradient of the full table.

    Hint

    For the second part, write a batch gradient as an average over its \(B\) examples and count how many times an example appears.

Practice

  1. practice Run the mini-batch loop of section 4 with \(B = 1, 4, 16, 64, 268\) and the same seed. Print the loss after 5 epochs for all five, with the numbers of steps. Make a small table and say which batch size is best per epoch.

  2. practice Change the loop to use the squared error through the sigmoid, with the gradient \(2(p - y)\,p\,(1 - p)\,x\). Start at \((w, b) = (-4, 2)\) with full batches and \(\eta = 0.5\). Print the loss and the share of sharks called right at steps 50, 100, 150 and so on up to 500. The share stays at one value for hundreds of steps. What is that value, how does it compare with the share of mature sharks in the data, and near which step does the run leave it?

  3. practice Build the cross-entropy landscape of the spadenose sharks in NumPy: a grid of 71 values of \(w\) from \(-6\) to 8 and 56 of \(b\) from \(-5\) to 6. Use np.argmin to find the lowest grid point, and compare it with \((4.61, 2.48)\). Load the lengths and labels from catch.csv, and scale the length.

Think deeper

  1. open SharkCam trains on photos, and a batch of 256 photos does not fit in the memory of a Raspberry Pi or a small graphics card. What would you do? Think about smaller batches, adding up several small batches before a step, and what these choices do to the noise and to the learning rate.

  2. open A friend says: "Squared error worked for my classifier once, so cross-entropy is a myth." Design a small experiment that tests the claim on the sharks. What would you vary, what would you keep fixed, and which result would change your mind?

  3. open Two training runs of the same network from different random starts reach the same accuracy but have different weights. In the one-hidden-unit landscape, why can this happen, and what does it mean for any claim of the form "this weight matters"?

Come back later

Try these after two days and again after a week, before you open the answers.

A model gives probability 0.8 to the true class and a second model gives 0.2. Compare their cross-entropy, and say which of the 0.7 ideas this is. (0.7)

\(-\ln 0.8 = 0.223\) and \(-\ln 0.2 = 1.609\). The loss is the surprise of the true answer: the less probability the model gave it, the larger the loss.

In A2 a learning rate that is too large makes the path bounce across a narrow valley. Where did you see that in this chapter, and what limit does it break? (A2)

In the one-hidden-unit landscape, whose valleys are long and narrow: at a learning rate of 0.3 or more the path bounces and settles at a higher loss. The limit is \(\eta < 2/k\), where \(k\) is the curvature across the valley (0.6).

The sigmoid has a slope of 0.0003 at \(z = 8\) (B1). Which two things in this chapter are explained by that number?

The tiny push of squared error when the network is confidently wrong, and the plateau of the squared error landscape. Both come from the factor \(p(1-p)\), which is the sigmoid's slope.

  2. Masters, D. and Luschi, C. (2018). Revisiting small batch training for deep neural networks. arXiv:1804.07612. arxiv.org/abs/1804.07612. Mini-batches of 2 to 32 gave the best test performance in their tests.
  3. Bottou, L., Curtis, F. E. and Nocedal, J. (2018). Optimization methods for large-scale machine learning. SIAM Review 60(2), 223–311. doi:10.1137/16M1080173, arXiv:1606.04838. A review of stochastic gradient methods. Only the abstract was read.
  4. Karpathy, A. (2019). A recipe for training neural networks. karpathy.github.io/2019/04/25/recipe. The check that the loss starts near \(-\ln(1/K)\), and the advice to overfit a single small batch.
